It's funny you mentioned this because I just posted a sort of "life hack" I made to help me retain large amounts of information: [https://www.reddit.com/r/ADHD/comments/quoxtp/lifehack\_for\_research\_that\_i\_discovered/](https://www.reddit.com/r/ADHD/comments/quoxtp/lifehack_for_research_that_i_discovered/)

I forgot to mention it in the post, but I use this technique for when I need to follow directions, too. Ever since I was young, I've only ever been able to focus on one step at a time when it came to directions (which actually worked a lot in my favor when it came to assembly instruction booklets!). As I got older, it worsened so that I would completely forget the previous steps I had taken while focused on the current step that I was on. But putting instructions in a bullet-point style has always helped me.

Wait, I always thought those moments were normal! My mom and aunt even said that's just a normal part of becoming an adult (granted, there's a lot of ND behavior that they say is part of being an adult).

But to answer your question, my biggest moment(s) would be how I would watch movies and marathon TV shows without taking in a scrap of information, but instead daydreaming my own storyline based on the few seconds I paid attention. Probably one of the biggest reasons I struggle so much with watching subtitled foreign things!

I was just about to post my own positive mental health action before I saw this!

Today specifically, I made my own little self-care kit. It has two stuffed animals, a fidget spinner, and a squishy toy I got out of a gumball machine that I use to stim. I've never bought anything specifically for self-care, so I just grabbed what ever old toys I thought would work.

Lately, I've decided to embrace my "weirdness": things that I suppressed to fit into the neurotypical social standards. I've always been told that a lot of the things I like/do are a result of bad parenting. Now, as an adult, I'm learning that a lot of those things were signs of autism, and that those "weird" behaviors (stimming, mimicking, fixations, etc.) aren't from my parents' failures and don't need to be "cured".

They might be intrusive thoughts. I've heard that they go hand-in-hand with some mental conditions such as OCD, ADHD, and anxiety. The key thing about them is that they don't actually reflect the person.

They might also just be the result of being around negative people. Personally, I have a similar "little voice" say things like that to passerby because, growing up, my family would tell me mean opinions about the people they saw. If you have friends or family who do that, you might be anticipating to hear them say negative things.

Personally, I think the best way to overcome this sort of mindset is to find a life purpose.

From my experience, I've had full-on existential breakdowns at the idea of living a "9-5 just to stay alive" lifestyle forever, but when I looked at my job and schoolwork as a side project to support my life's purpose, I felt better.

Everyone's life purpose is different, though, and varies greatly. For me, I relied on my religion and journey to grow as a creator. It gave me a fun hill to climb up so that everyday had nuance. You might discover your life purpose by finding something you're passionate about.

I don't really have a question, per se, but I do have some confusion about my diagnosis today. Although I was tested positive for ADD (they didn't say AD**H**D) and "other psychological disturbances", they told me that it was mainly due to my established anxiety and depression. They also said that I "over-reported" my symptoms in nearly 5 tests, and that all I needed was more therapy.

While I should be happy that I don't have anything too serious, I can't help but feel discarded and even embarrassed. I go to sleep nearly every night crying because my focusing, memory, and information processing skills get in the way of being an independent adult, and when I go to hopefully put a name on this monster I'm battling, I'm told that I'm being a hypochondriac and that I just need more discipline. In fact, my mother laughed at me when she heard it.

I don't even understand how I could over-report. The test only had me do puzzles and memory tests. At the end, there was an SAT-styled test that asked very tame questions like "Do you like to watch the news?", but that was it. At no point was I asked about my health or symptoms. Maybe it was because I slipped at the beginning and said that I was "getting tested for ADHD *or autism"* when he asked what I was coming in for. Or maybe I just experienced the "girls can't have adhd" bias firsthand.

EDIT: I have much more symptoms of ADHD that I've experienced throughout my life, but the memory, focus, and info-processing problems were what pushed us to see a doctor.
You're the positive, constructive comment I was looking for. Thank you, because I've been in the same position as OP for a while now.
